Monday morning. Cycle-time report. Override log. Did the agent hold, or did the human catch it?

That’s the job. Not the prompt — the gate.

I’m the named human on the release. When the agent gets it wrong on a credit pack or document check, my name is on it. That’s not a title. It’s a governance artifact.

The demo is 10%. The override pack and the Monday cycle-time review is the other 90%.

If you're hiring for AI enablement, ask one question:
"What's in your override pack?"

🚀 API Testing: Swagger + Postman — Two Tools, Two Different Jobs
A common question in API testing interviews is:
“What is the difference between Swagger and Postman?”
The simple way I remember it:
📘 Swagger / OpenAPI → Understand the API
🧪 Postman → Test the API
With Swagger, QA engineers can understand:
✅ API endpoints
✅ HTTP methods
✅ Request & response schemas
✅ Required parameters
✅ Authentication details
✅ Status codes
With Postman, we can go deeper:
🔹 GET / POST / PUT / DELETE testing
🔹 Positive & negative scenarios
🔹 Headers & authentication
🔹 JavaScript assertions
🔹 Environment variables
🔹 Collections & test suites
🔹 Newman automation
🔹 CI/CD integration
🔄 Real-world QA workflow
Swagger → Understand the contract → Postman → Functional & negative testing → Assertions → Newman → CI/CD → Database validation

💡 The key takeaway:
«Swagger tells you what the API is supposed to do.
Postman helps you verify whether it actually does it correctly.»
For a QA engineer, knowing both gives a much stronger understanding of API testing and automation.

👇 QA Engineers:
What do you use more in your projects — Postman, Swagger, or both?

I have been thinking in the recent past...Do humans and agents browse the web the same way? IMHO I don't think so. 

AI agents need more than a list of ranked links. They need web infrastructure that can gather context, verify evidence, and connect information across multiple sources. 

Recruiting GovTech talent is not a keyword-search problem. It’s an agent-browsing problem.
The engineer who can modernize a mission-critical system may never write “GovTech” in their headline.
The real evidence is scattered:
1-A conference talk on secure cloud migration 
2-GitHub work that shows technical depth 
A case study on modernizing citizen-facing services 
3-A public-sector contract, architecture write-up, or open-source contribution 
Signals that they can operate in regulated, high-accountability environments

A conventional search workflow returns a ranked list of links and assumes a human will open tabs, connect the dots, assess credibility, and decide what matters. That is human browsing.

Agent browsing should work differently (all about tokenomics, context windows, etc).
Give an agent an objective such as:
“Find senior platform engineers with public evidence of cloud modernization, security-minded engineering, and experience delivering software in complex public-sector environments. Show the evidence, source it, flag gaps, and do not infer sensitive attributes.”
Now the work is not “search once and summarize.” It is:
1-Decompose the objective into multiple evidence paths 
2-Search and read across many sources in parallel 
3-Resolve whether the signals actually refer to the same person 
4-Extract the relevant evidence and not just URLs 
5-Produce an auditable candidate brief with citations and confidence gaps 
6-Monitor for new signals over time

That is why companies building agents on top of a conventional, Google-style link index may miss the throughput and depth recruiting agents need.
A human may investigate 10 tabs sequentially (didn't we agree context switching is bad for us?). A recruiting agent needs to pursue hundreds of targeted research paths, extract the highest-signal evidence, and return a structured short list that a recruiter can validate.

The goal is not to automate hiring decisions ( Don't we have enough of that already?)
We already have evidence that humans need to be in the drivers seat where agents drive the effort and humans drive the outcome. In the recruiting context that means to give recruiters back the time to do the human work: build relationships, evaluate judgment, understand motivation, and make fair decisions.

For GovTech, that difference matters. We do not need more keyword matches. We need better evidence of mission-fit and demonstrated capability.

"Product Manager" sounds like one job. It is not.

A growth PM lives in funnels and experiments. A good week is a test that moved activation, or one that killed a pet idea early.

Platform PMs have customers too, they just happen to be the internal developers calling their APIs. Success looks like other teams shipping faster without filing a ticket.

An AI PM owns evals and model tradeoffs. Half the roadmap is deciding what "good enough" means when the output is never the same twice.

A B2B PM lives in sales calls. The roadmap works like a contract, and a slipped date can cost a renewal.

Same title. Very different work.

The gap shows up most at hiring time. A job post that only says "Product Manager" hides which of these the team wants, and interviews often test generic frameworks instead of the variant they need. A growth PM asked to defend enterprise roadmap commitments can look weak in the loop while being very good at a different job.

If you are applying, work out which of the four the JD really describes before tailoring anything. If you are hiring, put the variant in the title.

Which one are you?

The conversation around Excel in 2026 is shifting from "can you build a pivot table" to "can you engineer a spreadsheet that an AI agent can reliably consume." The latest releases, including Agent Mode and Formula Completion, are not just quality-of-life improvements. They represent a fundamental change in how we should think about spreadsheet architecture.

The non-obvious observation: the most critical skill for an Excel power user is no longer memorizing every function or keyboard shortcut. It is designing spreadsheets with a clear, deterministic data contract. If your spreadsheet is a tangled web of manual cell references, volatile functions, and hidden sheets, an AI agent will struggle to parse it. The new Formula Completion and improved error handling features work best when the underlying model is clean, normalized, and annotated.

For teams adopting the 2026 Excel 365 features, the practical takeaway is to treat your workbook like a data product. Define clear input and output zones. Use structured references and named ranges. Avoid volatile functions like INDIRECT and OFFSET unless absolutely necessary. The AI assistant is only as good as the spreadsheet it is crawling. A messy workbook produces messy, unreliable suggestions.

The real power of the new formula-based import functions and expanded AI assistance is that they reduce the friction between raw data and actionable insight. But this only holds if your data pipeline into Excel is already clean. If you are still pasting data from multiple sources with inconsistent formatting, you are handcuffing the AI before it starts.

For my own work, I focus on building Excel models that are "agent-ready." I define a clear metadata layer, standardize input schemas, and use Excel Tables as the foundation for any data source. This allows me to leverage the new features for rapid prototyping and scenario analysis without worrying about broken references or silent errors.

Recruiters and hiring managers: I bring deep experience in architecting robust, AI-compatible Excel models that accelerate decision-making without sacrificing accuracy. If your team needs someone who can bridge the gap between traditional spreadsheet expertise and the modern AI-assisted workflow, I would welcome the conversation.

Most enterprise AI programs do not stall because the model is weak.

They stall because no one owns the decision when the system is confident and the human is uncomfortable.

Boards talk about principles.

Teams ship copilots and agents.

Then a high-stakes recommendation appears:

A credit exception.
A hiring shortlist.
A contract clause.
A production change.

And the room goes quiet.

Who can override it?

Who is accountable if the override is wrong?

Who reviews the exceptions next week?

In too many organizations, those answers exist as hallway consensus rather than as a named control.

That gap is the real governance problem.

Adoption is outrunning ownership.

CIOs can be held accountable for systems they did not authorize.

Business units can deploy faster than IT can inventory.

And eventually, “the AI decided” becomes an unofficial operating model.

Until an incident makes that model impossible to defend.

The practical distinction is simple:

Capability is not authority.

An AI system can retrieve.

It can recommend.

An agent can even act.

But authority is something different.

Authority is the explicitly defined right to:

Approve.
Pause.
Override.
Stop.

And it requires evidence that someone actually reviewed the difficult cases.

A practical control

For the next AI use case that touches money, people, or customers, create a one-page decision-rights card before scaling it.

Define:

• Who authorizes the system to operate in the workflow
• Who can override an output, and within what window
• Who owns the recurring exception review

If you cannot identify those three roles without calling a meeting, the use case may have capability — but the operating model has not established authority.

The question is therefore not only:

“Can the AI make this decision?”

It is:

“Who has the authority to decide what happens when the AI is wrong?”

Because governance is not proven when the system produces the expected answer.

It is proven when someone has the authority, evidence, and accountability to handle the unexpected one.

The Broken Social Contract of Hiring: Ethics in the Modern Job Market
The modern job search has devolved into a high-stakes transaction where trust is replaced by gamesmanship. With economic uncertainty and high living costs making every career move critical, both job seekers and employers are caught in an adversarial system.
1. The Applicant’s Dilemma: Leveraged Candidates
Some job seekers complete lengthy interview loops with no intention of accepting the job, using offer letters solely as leverage to secure counteroffers from their current employers.
Impact on Employers: Teams waste significant time, budget, and resources interviewing candidates who aren't serious.
Collateral Damage: Serious, qualified applicants are put on hold or rejected while non-serious candidates negotiate.
The Reality: Counteroffers rarely work long-term—79% of employees who accept a counteroffer still leave within 18 months.
2. The Employer’s Offense: Ghost Jobs
Companies frequently post "ghost jobs"—openings listed publicly with no intent to hire external candidates—to build talent pipelines, signal growth to investors, or placate overworked teams.
Impact on Applicants: Job seekers waste effort tailoring resumes and completing assignments for non-existent positions.
The Data: Research shows 4 in 10 companies posted fake job listings in the past year, and 85% of those hiring managers interviewed candidates for roles they never planned to fill. Overall, 20% to 30% of active listings are ghost jobs.
3. The Algorithmic Gatekeeper: AI & ATS
Automated applicant screening creates a massive barrier between talent and hiring managers.
[Applications Submitted] ──> [AI / ATS Parsing Filters] ──> [75% Filtered Out] ──> [Human Review (25%)] 
Automated Rejection: Roughly 98% of Fortune 500 companies use Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), which filter out up to 75% of resumes before a recruiter sees them.
The Disconnect: Keyword-matching algorithms frequently discard top talent over formatting issues or missing buzzwords.
The Feedback Loop: Applicants use AI tools to mass-apply, driving employers to set harsher automated filters—creating an endless cycle of noise.
Restoring Transparency
For Job Seekers: Be transparent about your intentions. Seek market adjustments directly from current employers rather than wasting another company's resources.
For Employers: Keep job boards accurate, state salary ranges upfront, and ensure human oversight in candidate evaluation instead of relying strictly on automated filters.

I feel qualified to comment here, this is my everyday conversation.

Perhaps people that stay are complaining, whilst high performers are freely moving, with confidence, to greener pastures.  Often tapped on the shoulder from recruiters or their networks.

You used to want 5-10 years out of a permanent hire (1, 2, 3 roles), now getting 2-4 years of contribution is generally accepted on a CV and considered a win.  I think people have far less patience, they want promotions, growth, development now, and aren't going to stick around and wait.  Particularly those under 30, if they aren't moving up in 12-18 months, they'll look elsewhere.  I can introduce you to several right now in that boat.

As for caution from employers on growing headcount... can't say that is widespread - there are always growing and shrinking companies.  I haven' heard 'hiring freeze' a single time...yet, most hiring seems to be permanent, not contract/temporary (which would be a sign of caution), and roles that become vacant are being refilled immediately (not wait and see or absorbed by others).  

Our national news is dominated by the east coast, and fair enough, the readership is like 80% over there.  But in WA, a different story in a different world is happening at the same time.  We are still in our strong market phase (let's hope it continues).

AI isn’t just changing jobs. It may be changing the career ladder itself.

I was reading CBC’s recent piece about how Canada’s biggest banks are adopting AI, and it made me think about this from the perspective of someone who has spent nearly two decades in recruitment.

Companies are finding ways to automate work that once required significant human time. And from a business perspective, that makes complete sense. If technology can make a team faster, reduce repetitive work and allow people to focus on higher-value decisions, companies should be exploring it.

But here’s the question I keep coming back to:

“What happens to the entry-level jobs that used to develop our future senior employees?”

Most of us didn’t start our careers doing strategic work.

We started with the repetitive work.

The administration. The research. The documentation. The spreadsheets. The first drafts. The basic analysis. We learned by doing those things. Eventually, we developed the judgment and experience to take on bigger responsibilities.

Now AI can perform more of that foundational work.

So maybe companies shouldn’t just be asking:

“How many people can AI replace?”

A better workforce question might be:

“If AI changes the work, what kind of people do we need now?”

That is a conversation we’re increasingly having at Targeted Talent.

Sometimes the answer isn’t another permanent employee.

It could be a specialized contractor who brings expertise for a particular project without adding permanent headcount.

It could be an agile team assembled around a specific business outcome.

It could be an experienced professional who knows how to use AI to accomplish what previously required several people.

Or it could mean looking beyond a traditional résumé and hiring for adaptability, judgment, problem-solving and the ability to learn.

That’s where I believe recruitment has to evolve too.

Our job shouldn’t simply be to fill yesterday’s job descriptions.

It should be to understand what the business is trying to accomplish and then determine what talent: permanent, contract, project-based or otherwise, can help accomplish it.

AI will undoubtedly change the workforce.
But companies will still need people.

The more interesting question is going to be:

Which people, with which skills, working in what kind of model?

That’s the conversation I’d love to have with more business leaders.

If you’re looking at your 2027 plans and wondering whether you have the right people to execute them, feel free to reach out to me or the team at Targeted Talent.
